title: MahaREAT Orders Purva Oak to Refund ₹1.85 Crore Over Delayed Thane Flat Possession
meta_description: Maharashtra's real estate appellate tribunal ordered Purva Oak to refund a Thane buyer with interest, holding an early complaint does not bar relief.
bench: Bench composition not confirmed in available reporting
case_name: Homebuyer v. Purva Oak Private Limited (One Park Avenue, Ghodbunder Road, Thane)
citation: Appeal against MahaRERA order of 2021 dismissing the original complaint as premature; MahaREAT order dated 9 October 2026 (appeal number not confirmed in available reporting)
body: A homebuyer in Purva's One Park Avenue project on Ghodbunder Road, Thane, filed a complaint with MahaRERA well before his contractual possession deadline, betting that the deadline would be missed anyway. MahaRERA dismissed the complaint in 2021 as premature, reasoning that a complaint filed before the deadline had even arrived could not yet claim relief for delay. The buyer appealed, and the Maharashtra Real Estate Appellate Tribunal has now reversed that dismissal, ordering a refund of close to Rs 1.86 crore with interest.

The Tribunal's order, dated 9 October 2026, works out the refund precisely: Rs 1,85,99,612, less Rs 14,10,604 the buyer had already paid in taxes connected with the purchase, carrying interest at the State Bank of India's highest Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate plus two percent, payable within thirty days. It also directed execution of a cancellation deed within forty-five days so the buyer can claim back the taxes paid to the authorities, and awarded Rs 25,000 in litigation costs.

Deducting the taxes from the refund rather than leaving the buyer to chase a separate refund from the tax authorities is a practical touch that matters more than its size suggests. Buyers who cancel a flat purchase often discover that recovering stamp duty or registration charges already paid is its own small ordeal, running on a different timeline and before a different authority than the one hearing the builder dispute. By tying the refund arithmetic to a cancellation deed executed within forty-five days, the Tribunal gave the buyer a single, time-bound mechanism to get both halves of his money back rather than two separate fights.

The timing point raised by MahaRERA's original dismissal is the one with the most reach beyond this one buyer. MahaRERA's original logic, that a complaint filed ahead of the possession deadline cannot complain of delay, treated the deadline as a fixed finishing line that had to be crossed before a grievance became ripe. The Tribunal did not accept that the proceedings had to freeze at the moment of filing. By the time the appeal came to be decided, the deadline had long passed and the flat was still undelivered, and the Tribunal held that later development could not be ignored simply because the complaint predated it.

Purva Oak, the company now running the project, tried a separate defence: it said it only took over the project later and should not answer for the earlier developer's broken promises. The Tribunal was not persuaded. MahaRERA had approved the transfer of the project to Purva Oak on 13 August 2024, and Section 15 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act fixes the consequence of that kind of approved transfer: the incoming promoter steps into the outgoing one's shoes and carries forward its contractual and statutory obligations, arrears included.

The Tribunal also dealt with the registered completion date, which the RERA records showed had been extended to 30 April 2027. Developers routinely point to such extensions as proof that no delay has occurred yet. The Tribunal read the extension differently: a registration extension changes what RERA's own records say about the project's timeline, but it does not rewrite or alter the separate contractual obligations the buyer and the original developer agreed to in the Agreement for Sale. Those obligations, and the possession date fixed in them, stood on their own.

Buyers facing a stalled handover after a project changed hands now have a concrete precedent to test against: liability for the old developer's delays travels with the project once MahaRERA has approved the handover, and a buyer does not lose the right to complain merely because their complaint arrived at the Tribunal's door earlier than the clock on their possession date had technically run out. For a sector where project transfers are becoming more common as stressed developers hand off half-finished towers to better-capitalised buyers, this is one of the clearer statements yet on where the old liabilities land once the paperwork changes hands.
why_it_matters: Homebuyers often hold back from complaining until well after a possession deadline has passed, worried an early complaint will be thrown out as premature. This ruling says a complaint need not wait that long, and a developer's later default can be weighed even if filing came first. Incoming developers who take over a stalled project through an approved RERA transfer also inherit the previous developer's delay liability under Section 15, so due diligence before taking over a project becomes directly relevant to pricing that risk.
card_summary: MahaREAT ordered Purva Oak to refund ₹1.85 crore plus interest to a Thane buyer, holding an early-filed complaint can still succeed and an incoming promoter inherits the outgoing developer's delay liability.
card_tip: Buying into a project that changed hands mid-construction? Check whether MahaRERA approved the transfer; under Section 15 RERA, the new developer inherits the old one's delay liability.
verification_notes: The refund figures (Rs 1,85,99,612 less Rs 14,10,604 in taxes, SBI highest MCLR plus 2% interest, 30-day payment window, 45-day cancellation deed, Rs 25,000 costs), the project name, the 2021 MahaRERA dismissal as premature, the 13 August 2024 transfer approval, Section 15 reasoning, and the 30 April 2027 registered completion date are all confirmed by LiveLaw's report; Free Press Journal independently confirms the refund order, the amount (rounded to Rs 1.85 crore), the project and location, and the October 2026 timing. The appellant homebuyer's name and the appeal number were not disclosed in either report and are left out rather than invented. Free Press Journal's rounded figure (about Rs 1.85-1.86 crore) and LiveLaw's exact figure are treated as consistent rounding, not a conflict.
